Caribou.wildlife_intro:
Caribou sits in the middle of working potato ground, and the animals here live on the edge between field and forest. Groundhogs burrow under barns, sheds and field-edge banks, striped skunks dig for grubs in lawns and settle under porches, and raccoons raid outbuildings and find their way into attic spaces in older homes. Bats use farmhouse attics and barn lofts through the summer, red squirrels work the spruce and fir edges, and porcupines and fishers pass through the woods lots behind the farms — fishers are the usual suspect when chickens or barn cats go missing.

The season turns hard and early this far north. Our crew does a lot of fall sealing work before snow loads the roofs, then spring cleanouts when buildings closed since October are opened again. Wood heat is common, and stacked firewood against the house gives mice and squirrels a ladder to the eaves. Beaver flooding on the small streams is handled within Maine's permit rules, and exclusion and repair — not promises about moving animals — are what keep a Caribou property quiet.

Fort Fairfield.wildlife_intro:
Fort Fairfield is farming first, and its wildlife work is farm work. Groundhogs undermine barn floors, shed foundations and field-edge banks all over town, skunks den under porches and dig up lawns after grubs, and raccoons get into grain, garbage and the occasional attic. Bats summer in farmhouse attics and barn lofts, and where the Aroostook River and its brooks cross the farm roads, beavers dam culverts and flood low ground and driveways. Porcupines work the woods lots and chew on outbuildings through the winter.

The pattern here is seasonal in a practical way. Spring means groundhogs emerging and beaver water rising on the roads; late summer means skunks fattening up and bats at their most noticeable; fall means every small animal in the fields looking for a warm building. Our crew seals farmhouses and in-town homes, hardens outbuildings, and handles beaver problems under Maine's permit rules rather than with quick promises. Call us when you find the digging or the flooding — early jobs are almost always smaller jobs.

Fort Kent.wildlife_intro:
Fort Kent sits where the Fish River meets the St. John, surrounded by working forest, and wildlife pressure here comes straight out of the woods. Porcupines gnaw camp siding, outhouse woodwork and shed doors all along the river roads, red squirrels move into camp and home attics, and bats summer in older farmhouse attics and in camps that stand empty for months. Raccoons and skunks work the riverbanks and the edges of town, beavers plug culverts on the small streams, and fishers hunt the woods lots behind homes.

This is snow country in a serious way, and the rhythm of work follows it. Camps opened in May reveal a winter of squirrel and bat activity, and fall brings a rush of sealing jobs before the cold locks everything in. Our crew works as a Maine Animal Damage Control agent practice should — exclusion first, honest advice about what the permit rules allow, and no promises about relocating animals, which Maine restricts. Moose and bear sightings go to the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, not to us.

Houlton.wildlife_intro:
Houlton's older housing stock is its wildlife story. The big Victorian and early-1900s homes around Market Square have tall attics, aging trim and chimney flashing that bats and squirrels have used for generations, and raccoons find the same openings in winter. The Meduxnekeag River runs right through town, so skunks, raccoons and beaver activity follow the banks into nearby yards, and the farmland and woods lots on every side of town keep groundhogs, porcupines and red squirrels close to homes year-round.

Because Houlton winters are deep and long, animals that get into an attic in October may not be discovered until spring — and the damage by then includes insulation, wiring and stored belongings. Our crew inspects the whole roofline, not just the hole an animal was seen using, and bat work is done as exclusion only, timed to Maine rules. Call us in the fall for sealing work and you will save yourself the spring surprise that so many Houlton homeowners describe.

Madawaska.wildlife_intro:
Madawaska is the northernmost town in Maine, and its wildlife calls are a mill town's mix. Raccoons and rats work around the mill area and the older neighborhoods, skunks den under the porches of frame homes, and bats return each summer to the attics of the same older houses along the river. Out toward Long Lake and the woods roads, the calls change to camp problems — red squirrels in the eaves, porcupines chewing siding and steps, and beavers flooding camp roads where streams cross under them.

Winters on the St. John are long and cold, and a building closed in October can host animals for six months before anyone walks in again. Our crew sees the results every spring: fouled insulation, chewed wiring and bat colonies well settled in. We handle bat work by exclusion only, seal buildings properly in the fall when we can, and work within Maine's permit rules on beaver and other animals. If you are opening a Madawaska camp or buying an older home here, call us for an inspection before the animals announce themselves.

Bats settle into the attics and barn lofts of older farmhouses, raccoons work through sheds and grain storage, and striped skunks dig under porches and outbuildings across town. Red squirrels are a constant in attics near the tree lines, groundhogs burrow along field edges and under barn floors, and porcupines in the woods just outside town gnaw on shed siding, plywood and anything salted by winter road work.

Winters here are long and severe, so fall is busy as squirrels, mice and bats look for heated space before deep cold sets in. Many jobs start in spring, when camps and farm buildings that sat closed all winter are opened and a winter of damage is found at once. Our crew handles bat work as exclusion only, seals the entry points animals actually use, and deals with beaver flooding under the permit rules that apply in Maine.

Van Buren.wildlife_intro:
Van Buren is a quiet St. John River town where most properties sit close to fields, woods or water — usually all three. Raccoons and skunks work the riverbank and the village yards, bats settle into older home attics and camp lofts for the summer, and red squirrels are a year-round attic and camp problem in the woods outside town. Porcupines chew camp steps, siding and outhouses through the winter, groundhogs burrow at the field edges, and beavers keep the road crews and camp owners busy on the brooks.

Like everywhere in the Valley, the long winter shapes the work. Animals move into buildings in the fall, camps sit closed until late spring, and our crew spends May and June fixing what winter guests left behind. Wood heat, stacked firewood and older farmhouse construction all give animals their openings. We seal entry points, do bat work by exclusion only under Maine timing rules, and give straight answers about what can and cannot be done under state permits. Call us in the fall and most of the spring work never happens.
